### **1.6.2 Introduction** {#1.6.2-introduction}

Another step in the process of cleaning data is dealing with records with values that are either missing or extreme. Simply throwing away records with missing or extreme values is an approach that may work in certain situations. Understanding why values are the way they are is important in knowing when this would be appropriate. However, there are more sophisticated ways of dealing with these values. In this section we discuss missing and extreme values, reasons why they are missing or extreme, how that might influence your decision in dealing with them, and then provide tools for handling them.  
Introduction

### **1.6.3 Missing Data** {#1.6.3-missing-data}

While it is easiest to remove entire rows of data where any variables were missing, doing so can be damaging. Perhaps there is a reason why certain values are missing. If that is the case, then removing all the missing values can produce a model with significant bias. 

For example, suppose the target variable is readings from an instrument that measures the amount of a certain substance present in an environment. When the amount of the substance is below a certain threshold, though, the instrument returns an error. In this case, if you remove all instances where the instrument returns an error, you would be removing all data where the amount of the substance was low. When there is a systematic reason why data is missing, you may generate a model that is unable to make effective predictions when those conditions are repeated because it was not trained on those scenarios. 

Another example is an insurance application with a question about occupation. Possible responses might include “don’t know,” “prefer not to answer,” or no answer at all. Assuming everyone has an occupation, all three of these would be considered missing in that the actual occupation is unknown. But including all three of these as legitimate responses may be the right thing to do because future applicants might have these responses as well.  
Missing Data

### **1.6.4 Missing at Random** {#1.6.4-missing-at-random}

When there is no systematic reason that certain values are missing, this is called **missing completely at random (MCAR)**. When values are missing completely at random, it is more justified to remove those values from the data set without negatively affecting a predictive model based on that data. This might happen when a value is not recorded due to an error on the part of the data collection mechanism, such as a person not recording the data correctly. It could have happened to any observation regardless of anything inside the record with the missing data. 

When the reason data is missing has nothing to do with the value of the variable that is missing, but could be related to other aspects of a data set, the data is called **missing at random (MAR)**. In this case, throwing away observations with missing data may cause bias because there may be a reason certain individuals have missing data. Also, in this case there may be ways we can fill in those missing values with good guesses based on the rest of the data. Suppose there is data for Age and Previous Employer, where Previous Employer has some missing data. Someone who is young, may not have a Previous Employer to discuss, so they provide missing data. Then the age variable is somewhat indicative of whether or not Previous Employer is missing, and the data is missing at random. 

When data is missing because of what the values would have been if they were not missing, this is called **missing not at random (MNAR)**. The instrument detection is an example of this. Another example is drug testing. An individual might skip a drug test because they know they could fail, causing a missing data point specifically because of the value it would have been if it were not missing. Often this situation can be filled in as with MAR data, but perhaps there could be some other considerations, such as censoring or truncation. We will not be covering using censoring and truncation to deal with missing data in these modules, but these are a potential solution when data is MNAR.  
Missing at Random

### **1.6.5 Missing at Random** {#1.6.5-missing-at-random}

### **1.6.6 Permutation Test** {#1.6.6-permutation-test}

A permutation test is useful in applications where we are testing ordering or correlations. The process randomly reorders a variable to generate some statistic. You then repeat that process many times to generate a distribution of possible statistics. When you compare this distribution to your actual data, you will be able to see if order does matter. 

Let Variable *A* be a variable with missing data and Variable *B* have no missing data. A permutation test is conducted according to the following steps. 

1. Set the null hypothesis to be the data is MCAR and the alternative is that the data is not MCAR.  
2. Create a test statistic for the observed data, *T* \= *BM* – *BNM* where *BM* is the mean of Variable *B* when Variable *A* is missing and *BNM* is the mean of Variable *B* when Variable *A* is not missing.  
3. Randomly reorder either Variable *A* or Variable *B*.  
4. Calculate *Ri* \= *BM* – *BNM* on the reordered data set, where *Ri* is similar to *T*, but is calculated on the *i*\-th sampled permutation.  
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 a large number of times (perhaps 10,000).  
6. Obtain a 95% empirical confidence interval based on the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the values.  
7. If *T* falls outside the confidence interval, reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the values are not MCAR. If *T* falls inside the interval, there is not sufficient evidence to conclude that the missing values are not MCAR.

Permutation Test

### **1.6.10 Imputation** {#1.6.10-imputation}

When the data is not MCAR, it may be possible to fill in missing values with justifiable values. This is called **imputation**. While imputation may introduce additional sources of bias, it will often still be a better alternative than throwing out entire rows of data with any missing values. Imputation works best when there are many rows of data, as we will, in some cases, be using those other rows to help find the imputed values. 

We will look at the following imputation techniques: 

* Mean / Median  
* Regression  
* K Nearest Neighbors  
* Classification and Regression Trees

Imputation

### **1.6.11 Mean Imputation** {#1.6.11-mean-imputation}

The most basic form of imputation for numeric variables is to replace all missing values with the mean of the non-missing values of the same variable.  
Mean Imputation

### **1.6.12 Mean Imputation** {#1.6.12-mean-imputation}

One issue with imputation is that imputed values for integer values are not guaranteed to return an integer. For consistency of interpretable data, you could round the values to the nearest integer. However, for a predictive model, using imputed values that are non-integer will be fine. This issue will be seen again in other imputation methods.  
While a mean imputation is the simplest and fastest way to impute data, it does not add any information for the value being imputed. In fact, mean imputation assumes the data is MCAR, which means it can essentially be ignored. However, it is still useful as an alternative to throwing away the record because of the other variables that now get to be included in the data set. 

In some cases, if the variable is highly skewed it makes more sense to impute the median instead of the mean.

### **1.6.13 Regression Imputation** {#1.6.13-regression-imputation}

When the data is missing at random, there may be a significant amount of information in the other variables of the model to help us determine what the missing values may be. A simple way to do this is using regression imputation. This builds a regression model for a feature with missing data using only the complete rows. Then the missing data will be predicted and the predicted value will be imputed. 

In the production example we would take the following steps: 

1. Use only rows 1, 2, 4, and 5 to build a regression model to predict *Available\_Machines* using *Employees* and *Hours\_Open*.  
2. Using the values for the predictors in row 3, use the model to predict Available\_Machines.  
3. Impute the predicted value into the data set.

Note that if the model is being built to predict a target variable in the data set, that target variable should not be used for the imputation algorithm.  
Regression Imputation

While not seen in this example, another advantage is that while mean imputation would impute the same value for all missing data points in a variable, regression imputation returns different values for each. This may be important for a predictive model such as a decision tree where many values fixed at a single point, as would be the case for mean imputation, could cause clusters in the nodes that will artificially affect the model.

### **1.6.14 Regression Imputation** {#1.6.14-regression-imputation}

Regression imputation as done in CHUNK 5 has one drawback. Using deterministic predictions can lead to overfitting with regard to the interrelationships among the predictor variables. These predictions assume the fitted linear model is the true relationship between the variables and that there is no error in that relationship. The mice package includes three alternative approaches: 

* Add a random adjustment to each imputation based on the standard error from the regression model. Use **method \= "norm.nob"** to do this.  
* Use Bayesian estimation to incorporate both sources of variability. Use **method \= "norm"** to do this.  
* Use the bootstrap to incorporate both sources of variability. Use **method \= "norm.boot"** to do this.

All of these methods employ random numbers and hence a seed should be set if results should be reproducible. For this course, if regression imputation is used, it will be sufficient to use the version without incorporating randomness.  
Regression Imputation

### **1.6.15 KNN Imputation** {#1.6.15-knn-imputation}

Another approach to using the data to help predict missing values is using K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN). Essentially this approach defines a distance metric and determines the nearest K observations with non-missing data. Then the imputed value is the average of the values for those K observations. As with regression, this is better than imputing a mean or median. Compared to regression imputation, this may be easier to explain and a bit simpler for a non-technical audience but produces similar results. KNN imputation is typically slower for larger data sets.  
KNN Imputation

### **1.6.17 Categorical Imputation** {#1.6.17-categorical-imputation}

The methods presented so far require numeric data. When they are categorical, the approach will be different. For example, instead of imputing a mean, the mode can be imputed for a quick and simple approach. 

If the variable with missing values is binary, a logistic regression function could be used instead of a linear regression function. When there are 3 or more categories, a categorical regression model can be built. These are outside the scope of this module. 

For KNN imputation of a categorical variable, the algorithm will determine which rows are considered to be neighbors, and then instead of taking an average of its neighbors, it will find the mode of the nearest neighbor variables.

### **1.6.19 Categorical Imputation Python** {#1.6.19-categorical-imputation-python}

If the only missing values were categorical, then using **strategy \= "categorical"** imputes the missing data by randomly drawing from the complete data of that variable, meaning if 50% of complete values were “A”, 30% were “B”, and 20% were “C”, then that would create a distribution for the missing values. While this is not optimal as it does not use the other variables in the data set, it is the only option that is available when there are 3 or more categories in a variable. 

For binary variables, using **method \= "binary logistic"** will fit a logistic regression model for the missing values. The binary variables will need to be converted into 0s and 1s. Suppose there are multiple data types with missing values. Then the strategy argument should be a dictionary defining the method to use for each variable. For example, in the modified production data set, if you wanted to use regression for the *Available\_Machines* variable and logistic regression for the *Manager* variable, you would use **strategy={"Available\_Machines":"least squares","Manager\_On":"binary logistic"}**, where *Manager\_On* is a variable that is 1 when *Manager* \= “On” and 0 otherwise. In this way you can define exactly what method to use on each variable type. While you can use different methods that work best for the situation, when there are mixed data types with missing data, one suggestion would be to use regression for continuous variables, logistic regression for binary variables, and categorical for factors with 3 or more levels.

### **1.6.20 Missing Target Variable Observations** {#1.6.20-missing-target-variable-observations}

The goal of a predictive model is to use predictor variables to predict a target variable. When certain predictors are missing, we have seen several methods to impute the data. In many cases this is a superior alternative to throwing away an entire record, especially in cases where there are many variables. Suppose a record has 20 variables, only 1 of which is missing. There is a lot of information potentially being thrown out when the record is removed. Thus, imputation can be extremely useful in this case. 

Suppose that the target variable is missing for a record. Then imputation essentially becomes model prediction. Consider the regression imputation approach. In this approach, you use only complete records, build a model, and then predict the missing values. This is no different than just building the desired model on the complete records. Training a model should be done using only records with target variables.   
Missing Target Variable Observations

### **1.6.21 Missing Target Variable Observations** {#1.6.21-missing-target-variable-observations}

It is still concerning removing entire records, especially when the target variable is not missing completely at random. Since imputation is not an option, the only action you can take when you encounter a non-MCAR target variable would be to investigate the cause of its missingness. For example, suppose you are building a model to predict daily sales, and some days have missing values. Upon investigation you discover that the credit system was down on the days with missing values and sales were cash-only. This may have affected other variables in the data set, causing missingness of daily sales to be not missing completely at random. You have two options at that point. Perhaps you still throw out those data points because you only wish to use the model to predict sales on days with the credit system working. Or perhaps you still wish to include those days, in which case you may have other sources for the missing data. Imputation is not a valid option. 

Your decision path regarding a missing target variable is as follows: 

1. If the target is missing completely at random, you can throw out the data points, do not impute.  
2. If the target is not missing completely at random, investigate the cause of the missingness.   
   1. If the cause is determined to be an important case that needs to be accounted for in the predictive model, find the observation or a suitable substitute.  
   2. If the cause of the missingness is determined to be a case that does not need to be accounted for in the predictive model, the record can be thrown out.  
   3. If the missingness cause cannot be found, it is still better to throw out the records than to impute.

Missing Target Variable Observations

### **1.6.24 Identifying Outliers** {#1.6.24-identifying-outliers}

Both plots are effective in showing that there are some potential outliers, in this case in the right tail. It is more difficult to tell exactly which observations should be considered outliers. There are several methods of determining if a value is far enough away from the bulk of the data to constitute an outlier. The simplest is to use a *z*\-score on the data calculated by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the data. If the population is truly normally distributed, absolute values greater than 3 should be rare. The formula is   
![][image3]  
where *x̄* is the sample mean and *s* x is the sample standard deviation. 

This can be tricky because data sets with outliers are hardly ever normal. However, *z*\-scores can still be useful for understanding how far an outlier is in the context of the data. 

While the formula here is written using all the data, it may be more appropriate to remove the observation being tested when calculating the mean and standard deviation for the z-score. This process requires removing a single observation, calculating the mean and standard deviation of the remaining observations, and finding the z-score of the removed value. This is also called a Leave One Out or LOO *z*\-score. In smaller data sets, this method may be more accurate for detecting outliers.

### **1.6.26 Outlier Handling** {#1.6.26-outlier-handling}

When there is an outlier in a specific variable, there are a few remedies. 

1. **Transform:** Taking the log or square root of a variable will often reduce the extremity of the outlier and minimize their impact while modeling. When zeroes are present, the log of (data \+ 1\) could be used.  
2. **Remove:** If an outlier is deemed to be too extreme, its observation could be removed. This can be most appropriate if it is suspected the outlier is due to a recording or other human error.  
3. **Censoring:** It is possible that all that is needed to know for that particular variable is that the value is large. Providing a censored value, perhaps at a z-score of 3 or \-3, could still give the same information without a single observation impacting the results as much.  
4. **Replace with percentiles:** Again, maybe specific values aren’t as important as just knowing which observations have a higher value than another. This method transforms the full variable to a quantile of the data. The data would then be spread evenly between 0 and 1\.  
5. Ignore the outliers and include their observations in the model.

Outlier Handling

### **1.6.27 Outlier Handling** {#1.6.27-outlier-handling}

Which of these is most helpful depends on the situation. An important consideration is whether the variable is the target variable or a predictor variable. It would be more appropriate to change a predictor variable into a percentile than the target variable. However, it is common to take the log of the target variable. In fact, methods 3 and 4, truncated and percentile transformations, are not appropriate for transforming the target variable and should only be used for predictor variables. 

How you handle outliers also depends on how extreme the outliers are. Mild outliers may not merit any action at all whereas extreme outliers might. There is a possibility that the value is extreme but not an outlier and removing it could also remove useful information. The goal is to build a predictive model. Ideally, the data used to fit the model is representative of the data being used to predict in the future, meaning if these extreme values are important to be able to predict, then they are important observations to keep in the model. In this case consider using a transformation to decrease the effect of the extremity of the values, as this may help the model fit better for non-outlier values. However, if the outliers are not representative of the type of data you would like to predict with the model, perhaps they could be removed. The number of points that are determined to be outliers is important. If there are many outliers, it is possible that they are representative of a group that is important not to exclude or change. A few widely separated outliers would be more appropriate to leave out.  
Outlier Handling

### **1.6.28 DBSCAN** {#1.6.28-dbscan}

\[BEGIN LINK \-https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2021/06/understand-the-dbscan-clustering-algorithm/\]  
While looking at *z*\-scores for a specific variable is useful, it also seems that, unless that variable is particularly important, throwing out or changing an entire record based on a value of a single variable may be extreme. A method called Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) can determine outliers based on several variables. DBSCAN is a clustering algorithm that will discriminate between points that clearly fit within clusters of certain sizes and points that do not fit in any clusters. 

There are two main settings in a DBSCAN: 

* The distance at which two points are considered neighboring, called ε (eps when coding)  
* The minimum number of neighbors to be considered a cluster (minPts when coding)

The DBSCAN algorithm starts by identifying a core point randomly. If there are a minimum number of points within epsilon of the randomly chosen point, it forms a cluster. If not, it is considered “noise” which, when identifying outliers, can be interpreted as an outlier. All points within epsilon of the core point are included in that cluster. One way to interpret the results of this algorithm is that it will identify all points as outliers where you cannot find the minimum number of points within epsilon. More specific information and examples can be found at [https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2021/06/understand-the-dbscan-clustering-algorithm/](#bookmark=id.mk0ooi6871t4) 

This approach will only work on two or more continuous variables. A strategy may be to subset the data to only continuous predictor variables and use those in the DBSCAN algorithm to detect outliers as combinations of these continuous variables. 

\[END LINK\]  
DBSCAN

The communication section will discuss items such as when to explain more versus explain less. Part of this process is justifying decisions, both from a modeling perspective, but also from a data manipulation perspective. Give some thought to how you might communicate the work you did to prepare the data. 

A possible example of this report is available on the next page. This is not intended to be a full data exploration with summaries and figures of each variable.  
Case Study 1.2

### **1.7.6 Case Study 1.2: Report** {#1.7.6-case-study-1.2:-report}

\[BEGIN LINK \-https://cdn-files.soa.org/e-learning/atpa/atpa\_2\_7\_cs12.pdf\]  
A sample report is available for download ( [atpa\_2\_7\_cs12.pdf](#bookmark=id.i58fgeqd2e9q)).  
\[END LINK\]  
Case Study 1.2: Report

### **1.7.7 Case Study 2.1: Chiropractic Visits** {#1.7.7-case-study-2.1:-chiropractic-visits}

\[BEGIN LINK \-https://cdn-files.soa.org/e-learning/atpa/questionnaire.csv\]  
New Start Chiropractic (NSC) is trying to build a predictive model to predict how many visits a patient will have in a given year, using data from the individual's past visits as well as a questionnaire given to every new patient. The new patient data is in questionnaire.csv and contains information such as an individual’s age, sex, reason for coming, and some other medical information. The data on past visits was entered into a web application and is currently available in the file visits.xml, both of which are in the zip file downloaded at the beginning of this section. The historical visits data is all visits from 2015 to 2018 and includes information about the type of visit, how the visit was paid for, and if the individual rescheduled. 

The goal is to use past data to predict future visits, so the data in visits.xml will need to be manipulated to find both the target variable and the predictors. The target variable NSC wants to use is the number of visits an individual had in 2018\. NSC wants to use the information from both the questionnaire and the historical visit data as the predictors. They specifically wonder if the number of all visits prior to 2018 could be used as a predictor variable. The purpose of the model is both to understand what factors might influence an individual to come more often in a given year as well as to build a model to predict the number of visits an individual might have in future years. 

Write down the issues you find when you consider creating data for a predictive model according to the data files and the information provided. A possible solution is provided on the next page. Do not do any coding other than to examine the two data sets.  
\[END LINK\]  
Case Study 2.1: Chiropractic Visits

### **1.7.8 Case Study 2.1: Solution** {#1.7.8-case-study-2.1:-solution}

Here are a few possible issues to consider: 

1. The data in visits.xml contains records for each visit from any individual, not the number of times they visit in a year, but each visit is coded with the patient’s ID, which is also found in the questionnaire data. The data needs to be aggregated to provide the target variable, which is the number of visits in 2018\.  
2. The other variables in visits.xml can be used as well, but not in their current form. Perhaps using values such as the percent of visits that were normal versus extended, or the percentage of times an individual rescheduled could be used.  
3. There is a variable *year* in both data sets. In visits.xml, *year* records the year of the visit. In questionnaire.csv *year* records when the questionnaire was filled out. These variables need to be validated to make sure they are internally consistent.  
4. NSC wants to use the total number of all visits prior to 2018 as a predictor. We need to figure out if that makes sense for a predictive model or if there is a better variable to create using the past data.  
5. The questionnaire data is not complete. There are certain individuals who did not answer whether or not they have had surgery.  
6. The variable *why\_visit* has 15 different categories, but they are all some combination of 4 specific causes. Is there a way to split this variable into something with fewer levels?  
7. The variable *how\_heard* contains information about how the individual heard about NSC. There are a few significant levels of this variable but then some levels that do not occur often in the data. Can the number of levels be reduced?

Case Study 2.1: Solution

### **1.7.9 Case Study 2.2** {#1.7.9-case-study-2.2}

\[BEGIN LINK \-https://cdn-files.soa.org/e-learning/atpa/atpa\_2\_7\_r.rmd\]  
Perform coding tasks to solve the issues listed above. You do not need to perform a full data exploration with descriptions and figures for each variable. Solutions in R and Python are available on the next page. 

\[END LINK\]  
Case Study 2.2

### **1.7.10 Case Study 2.2: Solution** {#1.7.10-case-study-2.2:-solution}

\[BEGIN LINK \-https://cdn-files.soa.org/e-learning/atpa/atpa\_2\_7\_2\_r.rmd\]  
The solution is found in the Rmd files for this section ( [atpa\_2\_7\_2\_r.rmd](#bookmark=id.hxa7rw3g5mbr) and [atpa\_2\_7\_2\_python.rmd](#bookmark=id.ac0wrlmhzo3f)). These are a few specific notes based on the information provided: 

* Variables were created for the percentage of visits that were extended as well as the percentage of visits that ended with rescheduling another appointment.  
* One issue with using the total number of visits prior to 2018 as a variable in a predictive model is that the further new data gets from 2018, the less likely this variable will be as valuable. For example, imagine using this model to predict 2022 numbers. Using data from prior to 2018 for prior visits could be very inaccurate as client bases change and shift. Instead, we created a variable for the number of visits in 2017 specifically. In this case, the model could be used as is where that variable is the number of visits in the prior year. Regardless of the year, the information from the prior year will always be relevant.  
* The *year* variable was validated by examining the first year that a patient visited and matching it with when the questionnaire was filled out. Only 5 individuals out of 340, or about 1.4% did not match. This is fairly strong evidence that the year variable from both sources is consistent.  
* The vast majority of the complete data indicates that the individual has not had surgery. For this reason, all the missing data values were imputed as having no surgery. It would also be okay to use other imputation methods, such as CART or logistic regression.  
* Individual variables were created for each of the causes, where 1 indicates that that cause was listed and 0 indicated it was not.  
* The smaller levels in the *how\_heard* variable were combined. The new categories are referral, radio ad, internet search, and other.

\[END LINK\]  
Case Study 2.2: Solution

sections.title: **1.1.3 Module Introduction**  {#1.1.3-module-introduction}
sections.content:
This module introduces several examples of negative outcomes arising from modern technology, including big data, predictive models, and artificial intelligence. The main purpose of such examples is to illustrate that there could be negative unintended consequences due to reasons such as ill-will of agents, misuse, abuse, negligence of users, ignorance, cognitive fallacies, and underlying biases, both conscious and unconscious, of people. 

Especially in this information age, regulations have been evolving to prevent negative impact from these powerful new technologies. However, regulations are often slow to adapt to the fast-paced, evolving world. Also, regulations act as a boundary or limit rather than as guidance for day-to-day decision making. As such, ethical frameworks need to be considered and applied to provide guidance for the actuarial community. 

This module is intended to help you learn to use technology in a responsible way to provide value to stakeholders and the public. Two examples provide motivation for this material.  
Module Introduction

sections.title: **1.1.4 Example: Amazon Recruiting Algorithm** {#1.1.4-example:-amazon-recruiting-algorithm}
sections.content:
\[BEGIN LINK \-https://cdn-files.soa.org/e-learning/Predictive\_Analytics/Module\_1/BreastCancerWisconsinDataSet.csv\]  
Amazon’s hiring algorithm was considered biased against females, although information about the sex of the applicant was removed from the data. 

This example is summarized from the article “Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women” by Jeffrey Dastin (Dastin, 2018).  
\[END LINK\]  
Example: Amazon Recruiting Algorithm

Component Table3

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 3 |
| Tab 1 Title | What happened and how? |
| Tab 1 Text | What happened and how? |
| Tab 1 Content | In 2014, some engineers at Amazon started a project to develop a hiring algorithm that screened résumés and made decisions regarding whether or not an offer should be given to job applicants. Later in the development process, Amazon found that the results from the algorithm had a strong bias against female candidates applying for software development positions. Since Amazon had historically hired relatively more male than female applicants, the algorithm had been trained using that data. It essentially learned that males were better candidates based on the historical data. By using key words that separate males from females, the algorithm perpetuated the bias even without direct information about the applicant's sex. |
| Tab 2 Title | Resolution |
| Tab 2 Text | Resolution |
| Tab 2 Content | Amazon could not fix the problem even with its experience in the data analytics area. Removing sensitive fields from the data didn’t help as the algorithm was smart enough to find proxies for the applicant's sex. For example, the algorithm noticed that applicants who played sports generally played by females or who graduated from women's universities were historically not hired. This could lead to bias even though the applicant's sex was not directly recorded. Conversely, removing too much information (e.g., not recording the university attended) would penalize predictability. Amazon stopped this project after a year and claimed that the algorithm was never used in actual hiring. |
| Tab 3 Title | Lessons learned |
| Tab 3 Text | Lessons learned |
| Tab 3 Content | There are several lessons to be learned from this example:  Bias can easily be embedded in the data used to train the model, and simply removing relevant data fields in the input will not eliminate them. Outcomes based on bias and discrimination are rarely intentional. Yet, their impact is real. If biased algorithms are implemented, bias will be amplified, as biased and potentially discriminatory decisions may be made, new data will continue to be biased or include more bias, and bias will continue to be fed into the algorithm. This can lead to long-term disparate or negative impacts.  |

sections.title: **1.1.5 Example: Non-Transparent or Unexplainable Outcomes** {#1.1.5-example:-non-transparent-or-unexplainable-outcomes}
sections.content:
To understand whether results are fair, one should be able to test the fairness using certain attributes. Non-transparent models or unexplainable outcomes, even if the predictions are accurate, can be an issue. The following example illustrates why this can be a problem. 

In the criminal justice system, recidivism risk assessments are commonly used to predict a defendant’s likelihood of becoming a repeat offender. These tools are often based on advanced statistical models and trained on a variety of data points, including age, employment history, and prior criminal records. The scores derived from these tools are used across different stages of the criminal justice process; this varies by state. They influence decisions that affect defendants’ freedom, including setting bail, releasing on parole, and even in sentencing. 

There are concerns about the potential for bias and discrimination in these models. One challenge is the transparency of predictions. As pointed out in a Harvard Data Science Review article titled "The Age of Secrecy and Unfairness in Recidivism Prediction" about one such model, COMPAS, the authors noted the model’s complexity (it is based on up to 137 variables, many of which are collected from questionnaires and hence may be subject to data entry and other types of errors) and lack of transparency (the underlying formulas are proprietary). These factors pose clear challenges to ensuring fairness (Rudin, Wang, & Coker, 2020). It is especially important that models being used to make important decisions regarding people are as transparent as possible to protect the rights of individuals. This example is discussed in more detail in a later section. 

It is more difficult to diagnose and correct errors in a complicated model. In addition, the authors noted that faulty assumptions about a “black box” model lead to faulty conclusions. Transparency helps avoid these situations. Transparency provides two main benefits with respect to fairness. First, “it is easier to debate the fairness of a transparent model than a proprietary model.” Second, transparency provides an opportunity for remediation. With a life-changing decision, such as those impacted by recidivism risk assessments, a clear and verifiable explanation offers “procedural fairness.”  
Example: Non-Transparent or Unexplainable Outcomes

sections.title: **1.1.6 Overview** {#1.1.6-overview}
sections.content:
Overview   
This module discusses ethical principles and defines a framework into which these ethical principles can be categorized. Additionally, it introduces some notions related to protection from discrimination such as protected classes and proxy variables. It also covers key relevant standards of practice and regulations related to data protection, privacy, and anti-discrimination. The following tabs outline some of the key topics in this section. 

Click each tab to read more:

Component Table4

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 4 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | 1\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Content | Principles guide how we conduct ourselves both in our everyday lives and when the unexpected occurs. However, conflicts can arise between two different principles and a choice must be made between which to prioritize. An ethical framework can be defined to assist in the categorization of these principles; the framework used in this module divides ethical principles into three categories: fairness, safety, and accountability and transparency. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | 2\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Content | ASOPs provide guidance regarding the performance of actuarial services and communication of results. ASOPs covering communication, data quality, modeling, and risk classification are among the ASOPs related to the ethical principles and ethical framework used in this section.  |
| Tab 3 Title | 3\. Data Security and Privacy |
| Tab 3 Text | 3\. Data Security and Privacy |
| Tab 3 Content | The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union (EU) and California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in California are examples of data protection laws. They ensure that personal data possessed by organizations is sufficiently protected, for example, by encryption and access/transfer restrictions. In the context of a predictive modeling project, these laws will determine compliance requirements of any infrastructure or third party that you use for data processing/analytics (e.g., the cloud). Additionally, the laws and regulations influence the organization’s security policy, especially when personal data is concerned, due to the high cost and brand risk of potential breaches. |
| Tab 4 Title | 2\. Protection Against Discrimination |
| Tab 4 Text | 4\. Protection Against Discrimination |
| Tab 4 Content | Laws also protect customers' right not to be discriminated against and to be treated fairly. For example, the United States (U.S.) has anti-discrimination laws, such as the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act. |

sections.title: **1.1.7 Introduction**  {#1.1.7-introduction}
sections.content:
Due to the increasing use of big data and predictive models, there are more potential concerns and risks that need to be understood and considered. The technology associated with the unprecedented amount of data creates new challenges for us. Regulations and ethical frameworks have been emerging to respond to such challenges. The increased use of automation and predictive modeling results in less human review and intervention, creating a new class of ethical risks that were not previously encountered by the actuarial profession.\* This section provides an introduction to ethical values and ethical principles. 

As an example, insurance companies may consider collecting prescription history, credit history, geographic, biometric, and genetic data. To what extent can organizations legally and ethically collect this data? Is it acceptable to collect and use this data for pricing and underwriting an insurance contract even if a customer agrees? What is the right thing to do? This section provides a foundation and framework for participants to address these types of questions. An ethical framework guides why some decisions are more desirable than others; it also helps us to decide which data and models are permissible in a given situation. This is important, as some of these decisions are context-dependent. 

\* Because this material is intended as education for actuaries, we will often speak of the “actuarial profession.” However, the concepts in this module apply throughout the insurance industry and broader financial services.  
Introduction

sections.title: **1.1.8 Ethics**  {#1.1.8-ethics}
sections.content:
Generally, ethics refers to standards of behavior defining how individuals, a community, or society should act morally and responsibly in various situations. A succinct definition describes ethics as “the discipline dealing with what is good and bad and with moral duty and obligation” (Merriam Webster, 2020). A critical component of ethics is the obligation or responsibility to a larger group of people than an individual or organization and their direct relationships. This module focuses on the application of ethics in a professional setting.  
Ethics

sections.title: **1.1.10 Ethical Principles** {#1.1.10-ethical-principles}
sections.content:
Regardless of who we are, we order our lives by certain sets of principles. The principles may require a certain degree of interpretation, depending on the situation. Additionally, certain principles may conflict, and practitioners may need to balance the trade-offs. For example, a more robust and accurate model may be a black-box model, which may be a challenge to explain. A practitioner will need to decide which principles are a priority–a model that is more robust or one that is more transparent.  
Ethical Principles

sections.title: **1.1.11 Ethical Principles and Framework** {#1.1.11-ethical-principles-and-framework}
sections.content:
This module uses three broad groups to discuss ethical principles: 

1. Fairness,  
2. Safety,  
3. Transparency and Accountability.

Some of the principles may be connected and intertwined. For example, transparency and accountability are interrelated. If a model is not transparent and the cause of certain issues (such as biases) cannot be explained, it will be challenging to take responsibility and accountability. The framework used in this module is one example. It is not a definitive framework but will provide a foundation for the rest of the module. The focus is to apply the principles to guide considerations, rather than to have a definite rule to apply them. 

Other principles may be discussed in appropriate groups as needed. For example, robustness, accuracy, and privacy are discussed within the safety category. Although transparency and accountability are different principles, this module treats them as a group, as they are closely intertwined and interrelated. 

The focus of this section is to introduce these categories of the ethical framework and give some indications and examples of how they apply to predictive models and the data they use. We will return to the principles in this framework throughout the rest of the modules, showing how they apply to the various aspects of the data and modeling processes.   
Ethical Principles and Framework

sections.title: **1.1.12 Fairness** {#1.1.12-fairness}
sections.content:
**Fairness** refers to impartial and just treatment without favoritism or discrimination. Fairness often includes social context considerations ensuring individuals are treated consistently. Fairness is a principle where the aim is to protect human rights, such as dignity and equality, and the right not to be discriminated against. 

As fairness is defined under social context, there is no universal criterion or objective standard that applies. Determining fairness of a classification factor may depend on the domain, cultural, regulatory, and legal contexts as well as an individual’s viewpoint.  
Fairness  
Protected Classes and Proxy Variables   
\[BEGIN LINK \-https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10920277.2021.1951296\]  
Discrimination against certain groups, attributes, or categories, is illegal and regulated in many countries. Such groups are often referred to as **protected groups** or **protected classes**; examples of anti-discrimination laws and regulations are discussed later in this section. 

A **proxy variable** is a variable that is not a protected or sensitive variable, but is strongly correlated with a protected characteristic. As discussed earlier, Amazon built an algorithm using a predictive model to automate the hiring process. The hiring algorithm was considered biased against females even though the data did not include information on the sex of candidates. Removing sensitive fields from the data didn’t help, as the algorithm found proxies for sex. For example, the algorithm recognized when the applicant was on a women’s sports-team or graduated from a women’s college. 

An informative summary of some of the considerations regarding which variables should be considered protected or sensitive can be found in Section 2.2 of “ [The Discriminating (Pricing) Actuary](#bookmark=id.3vhi5ml4xife)” (Frees and Huang, 2021). This section of this paper is optional reading.  
\[END LINK\]

sections.title: **1.1.13  Fairness: Data** {#1.1.13-fairness:-data}
sections.content:
Applying the ethical value of fairness can lead to issues arising from both qualitative and quantitative aspects of using the data. 

Click on the tabs to read more.  
Fairness: Data

Component Table9

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 2 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | Data Quantity |
| Tab 1 Content | The amount of available data could lead to conclusions that are not considered fair. One example is that due to the imbalanced size of the data, minority data may have a higher level of inaccuracy due to having fewer and less credible data points, which may lead to larger data bias. Consider, for instance, Google’s photo tagging mishap that mislabeled people with dark skin (Vincent, 2018). One of the issues was that the model did not train enough on the underrepresented groups' pictures even though the sample may have been consistent with the racial make-up of the population. The issue is also prevalent in speech recognition for accents (Lopez-Lloreda, 2020). If credibility of data for under-represented groups is not assessed in a data source, use of the data source can lead to fairness issues with algorithms built using the data. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Data Quality |
| Tab 2 Content |  Data quality issues may arise from the following aspects, which require human input and judgment.  Sampling bias occurs when the sampled data are not representative of the population that is intended to be predicted, and no adjustment for this is made in the model. The bias may be due to the poor selection of data in that the source, timing, or purpose of the collected data may not be relevant to the purpose of the analytics exercise. For example, using U.S. data to predict outcomes for other regions or using data from the 1950s to predict current customer behavior are examples of how data may exhibit sampling bias. Implicit bias can occur in data creation. In implicit bias, the source data may include bias due to the way the data was created, or due to the bias implicit in human decisions that drove the response variable. An example of such bias is the framing effect, which is the tendency of a person’s decisions to be influenced by the manner (e.g., positive or negative) in which a situation is framed or presented.  |

sections.title: **1.1.14  Fairness: Analytics and Model** {#1.1.14-fairness:-analytics-and-model}
sections.content:
There are many aspects of the process of model building that require attention to the fairness of the models. There are also various ways in which we might measure or think about fairness in relation to predictive models. 

Click on the tabs to read more.  
Fairness: Analytics and Model

Component Table10

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 2 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | Analytics Fairness Measures |
| Tab 1 Content | One aspect of fairness in analytics or modeling refers to building models that do not discriminate against protected classes of people. However, there are many possible measures of fairness. For example, the fairness of a model may be assessed by examining average level of prediction for each group. Or fairness could be achieving similar rates of true positives or true negatives among groups. Further, the comparison could be performed at a group level or individual level to ensure modeled results are consistent across groups. These measures may not necessarily agree with each other (i.e., fairness based on one metric does not guarantee fairness based on the other metric). |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Design Considerations |
| Tab 2 Content | The fairness of the resulting predictive model should be considered in the design of models to prevent bias. For example, care should be taken to avoid usage of proxy variables that are dependent on or correlated to prohibited variables. An example is using a zip code that may correlate with race, ethnicity, national origin, or other protected classes. Checks should be done to ensure that a proxy variable is not being used. |

sections.title: **1.1.15 Fairness: Implementation and Governance** {#1.1.15-fairness:-implementation-and-governance}
sections.content:
Fairness can also be considered in the context of implementation and governance, which intends to ensure the overall process and model implementation, monitoring, and maintenance is fair and not biased or discriminatory. Even if fairness is considered in data collection, data selection, and the modeling stage, biased results may occur during the overall process and the implementation stage. 

Efforts to achieve fairness in implementation will be more successful if practitioners consider implementation aspects at the beginning of the project. Even though a feature may seem innocuous when building the model, in practice, it can end up responsible for a model unfairly discriminating based on the implementation. 

For an insurance example, even if the pricing or underwriting predictive models may have considered the data and model fairness ensuring that only actuarially sound factors were used, the marketing and commission strategy may promote or demote certain customer groups, leading to potential discrimination. 

Also, it is important to be aware of instances in which a model may have been carefully developed for one situation, but ultimately used for a different one; this can lead to bias and unintended consequences.  
Fairness: Implementation and Governance

sections.title: **1.1.16 Safety**  {#1.1.16-safety}
sections.content:
**Safety** refers to the operational and technical sustainability aspects of the data, model, and implementation. Safety can help protect aspects of human rights and public safety, such as the right not to be harmed, the right to privacy, freedom, the right to choose and autonomy, and the right for well-being and care. Safety may help to protect and prevent harm from misuse, poor design, unintended results, denial of autonomy, denial of rights, or breach of privacy. 

Accuracy and reliability are key components of safety considerations. Accuracy means that the data has no errors and the models produce correct results. Reliability means that a model, system, or prediction behaves consistent with intentions and expectations. It is not necessarily true that a model must be reliable if it is accurate. It is possible a highly complex model may be accurate but may be unstable and unreliable in interpretation. 

Robustness is a quality where accuracy and reliability are maintained under stressed, extreme, or unusual conditions.   
Security is protecting a model or a system against possible attacks that would breach integrity or privacy. 

Safety concerns arise during data collection, data selection, model building, and model implementation and governance processes.  
Safety

sections.title: **1.1.17 Safety: Data**  {#1.1.17-safety:-data}
sections.content:
Data accuracy is a component of safety and is a desired trait in the data extraction and collection process. A typical predictive modeling project requires extensive data wrangling. Data reconciliation and validation are done to ensure accuracy. 

Data privacy is also an aspect of data safety. Organizations may obtain customers’ personal information that should be kept safe. These organizations will need to consider how personal information is stored and used. Data may need to be encrypted and de-identified if required for specific purposes. Even if data is de-identified, the possibility of re-identification may cause harm or safety issues. 

For example, in 2006, Netflix held a contest that challenged researchers to find superior movie recommendation algorithms. Researchers were provided with de-identified datasets and a prize was announced. Two researchers from the University of Texas were able to re-identify a group of Netflix users very quickly by comparing rating information against public non-anonymous movie reviews on IMDb. A research paper was published describing how easy it was to re-identify an individual and, due to security concerns, Netflix had to cancel its prize and settled a lawsuit related to violation of the Video Privacy Protection Act. (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). 

Some data collected may be behavior-induced, such as variables related to lifestyle or wellness. Depending on how the data is collected, the behavior-induced data may affect accuracy, reliability, consistency, or integrity. An example is step-count data from a pedometer, that may have been affected by dishonest behavior (affecting the integrity of the data) or the device's inaccuracy (affecting the accuracy or reliability of the data).  
Safety: Data

sections.title: **1.1.18 Safety: Analytics and Model** {#1.1.18-safety:-analytics-and-model}
sections.content:
Analytical safety relates to analyzing the data in the model consistently as intended. Modeling requires an appropriate understanding of the problem definition, data, and algorithm. For example, causation and association should be distinguished. One would need to avoid misusing or misinterpreting some statistical features, such as Simpson’s paradox and P-hacking. 

Predictive models have an objective to maximize the accuracy of the predictive power given the data set. This accuracy is also an aspect of safety, as the predictive model aims to minimize any potential prediction error. While accuracy is a desired trait from a technical standpoint, the cost of false predictions can raise ethical questions. The model may be chosen to minimize the overall cost of the false predictions, given the costs of false positives (predicting as positive although that is not true) and false negatives (predicting as negative although that is not true). Models are not perfect, and there may be trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. 

A fire alarm is an example where the cost of false negatives (the alarm not going off if there actually is a fire) outweighs the cost of false positives (the annoyance of an alarm without a fire). This cost consideration results in a reasonably sensitive alarm that might warn of benign smoke coming from a cooking oven.  
Safety: Analytics and Model

sections.title: **1.1.19 Transparency and Accountability** {#1.1.19-transparency-and-accountability}
sections.content:
**Transparenc** **y** and **accountability** are ethical principles that apply before, during, and after developing models. 

Click to read more.  
Transparency and Accountability

Component Table11

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 3 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | Transparency |
| Tab 1 Content | Transparency refers to the quality of how the process is documented and disclosed, explained, interpreted, and communicated. Interpretability, explainability, and understandability are related principles. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Accountability |
| Tab 2 Content | Accountability refers to defining and allocating responsibility throughout the workflow. Responsibility may relate to owning the processes and the results and determining who will answer when questions arise. Accountability means that agents take responsibility and liability, and act with integrity. |
| Tab 3 Title | Interrelationship Between Transparency and Accountability |
| Tab 3 Text | Interrelationship Between Transparency and Accountability |
| Tab 3 Content | Transparency and accountability are closely interrelated as both relate to procedural aspects of modeling. If a model is not transparent and the cause of certain issues (such as biases) cannot be explained, responsibility and accountability will be challenging. Transparency of the process will help define who will be responsible for answering questions raised by a regulator or a customer. Auditability is a quality to track the actions throughout the process and see if procedures are repeatable. Auditability may not equal transparency or accountability but is interrelated with transparency (to document the process clearly), accountability (to indicate who did what), and stability or reliability (to ensure procedures are repeatable and results are consistent).  |

sections.title: **1.1.20 Transparency and Accountability: Data** {#1.1.20-transparency-and-accountability:-data}
sections.content:
Transparency, accountability, and auditability apply to data wrangling. Data wrangling, which includes data collection, merge, mapping, transformation, and conversion procedures, should be well-documented, and the team should be accountable for any issues with the data. The data process needs to be auditable to ensure it has clear ownership, is sound, and reproducible. 

Defining who owns the data relates to accountability. For example, data ownership might not be clear if the data is de-identified or transformed into metadata. Does the metadata belong to an individual or an organization that collected and processed the individual inputs? 

If one takes a photo of people at a public beach, who owns the picture? What, if any, kind of consent was necessary before or after taking the photo? If one publishes the unedited picture on a public website, what can a person in the photo claim? What right do the people in the photo have? Can the people in the picture claim ownership of the photo? Can the people in the picture claim to be de-identified? While local regulations may answer some of these inquiries, part of accountability relates to clarifying data rights and ownership and ensuring the data is handled in an ethical way. Accountability also means defining and clarifying the responsibilities of the data collector and the data processor in relation to such rights and ownership.  
Transparency and Accountability: Data

sections.title: **1.1.21 Transparency and Accountability: Analytics and Model** {#1.1.21-transparency-and-accountability:-analytics-and-model}
sections.content:
Explainability is the extent to which the workings in a machine learning algorithm can be explained in human terms. It means being transparent about what variables are used, the extent to which they drive the response, and how changing the inputs would impact the output. (U.K. Government Digital Service, 2020). 

Model explainability also refers to the ability to explain the model design, algorithm, assumptions, and inferences. Inferences include explaining a relationship between predictor variables and the predictions. Model explainability refers to an interpretation of the model and explanations for how the model is working as intended. 

Black box models may be referred to as such since the algorithms are too complex to be easily comprehended, people do not understand why or how the model works, or the drivers behind the results cannot easily be explained. From a regulatory perspective, black box models can refer to those where the model mechanics are considered proprietary, and the organization is not willing to submit them to regulatory scrutiny. Models built using more advanced machine learning methods may be very difficult to interpret due to the model structure. However, even simple models can sometimes be difficult to understand. While you may be able to trace through the algorithm, understanding the results and gaining insight into the predictors can still be a challenge.  
Transparency and Accountability: Analytics and Model

sections.title: **1.1.22 Transparency and Accountability: Implementation** {#1.1.22-transparency-and-accountability:-implementation}
sections.content:
Transparency and accountability issues also arise in implementation. Data collection, data analysis, model calibration, and model predictions are all performed by machines with the guidance of humans. Predictive modeling projects may automate the workflow of the processes (e.g., data extraction, data validation, and audit functions). Transparency requires that the process and outcomes are clearly documented and communicated, such that it can be repeated and audited. The analytics process includes the end-to-end process, e.g., data collection and selection, data processing, model selection and validation, model deployment and monitoring. Transparency as it relates to the outcome means the ability to explain and justify the effect of the model in relation to the business context, ethical values, and other ethical principles (e.g., fairness). 

Accountability requires that the process as well as the results are owned by humans, not machines. Using machines to perform calculations and orchestrate the workflow does not mean humans are exempt from responsibility. As such, accountability includes having sufficient controls in the automation. Human control may mean review, monitoring, and any other interventions (e.g., a kill switch that allows an operator to immediately shut down a machine even though it may damage it.). 

What should be done when issues arise in the predictive models? Both transparency and accountability are key considerations to address. Transparency of the model would help understand the source of the issues; transparency of the process would help communicate the issue with necessary stakeholders, and accountability allows responsible agents to take necessary actions.   
Transparency and Accountability: Implementation

sections.title: **1.1.23 Interrelations Between Ethical Principles** {#1.1.23-interrelations-between-ethical-principles}
sections.content:
In addition to independently considering each of the principles of fairness, safety, and transparency and accountability, it is also vital to examine how they are interrelated. There are many instances in which these principles depend on or reinforce one another. 

Click to read more.  
Interrelations Between Ethical Principles

| Tab 1 Text | Transparency and Accuracy |
| Tab 1 Content | Transparency is required to confirm accuracy. If organizations are not transparent with how models are being used and how models reach decisions, it is difficult to know when organizations are making mistakes. If consumers and policyholders can’t understand how models are determining rates and other decisions, then they won’t have an opportunity to correct inaccurate data. Transparency mitigates the risk of biased analysis. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Accountability and Accuracy |

Someone or a function within an organization needs to be assigned responsibility for model accountability. Knowing who is responsible for this data will assist in addressing how to verify accuracy, and how to address concerns. |
| Tab 3 Title | Interrelationship Between Transparency and Accountability |
| Tab 3 Text | Transparency and Fairness |
| Tab 3 Content | Like the relationship between transparency and accuracy, transparency is also required to achieve fairness. Companies should be transparent about the models they use; otherwise it is difficult to validate that the models are acting in an unbiased and fair way. One of the biggest repercussions of a lack of transparency is that consumers may not trust an organization. This lack of trust diminishes goodwill. |

sections.title: **1.1.24 Tensions Between Ethical Principles** {#1.1.24-tensions-between-ethical-principles}
sections.content:
There are also times when there are tensions or conflicts between ethical principles, in which some trade-offs must be made, or some balance struck. 

Click to read more.  
Tensions Between Ethical Principles

Component Table13

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 3 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | Transparency and Accuracy |
| Tab 1 Content | In general, increased transparency allows for more individuals to check various aspects of the algorithm and ensure that each step of the process is accurate. While transparency may lead to an increase in positive behaviors, transparency is not always feasible or desirable. For example, too much transparency may allow consumers to “game” the system, decreasing accuracy.  |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Explainability and Accuracy |
| Tab 2 Content | Sometimes in using analytics, we are faced with an ethical tradeoff between model explainability and model accuracy. For example, “black box” models, such as deep learning, may perform well with high accuracy in visual recognition tasks, but with the cost of low explainability. From an ethical perspective, more accurate models may lead to an outcome that is fairer, but the inability to explain a model leads to a lack of transparency to the consumer regarding the reasons behind their outcome (e.g., in pricing and underwriting). |
| Tab 3 Title | Interrelationship Between Transparency and Accountability |
| Tab 3 Text | Accuracy and Fairness |
| Tab 3 Content | An example of the tension between accuracy and fairness is the use of credit-based insurance scores in insurance ratings. In most states, insurance companies can use credit-based insurance scores to help predict how likely an insured will file a claim that will lead to a loss for the insurer. States generally regulate the use of credit-based insurance scores, and some states do not allow insurance companies to use your credit information at all. In terms of accuracy, the use of credit-based insurance scores in auto insurance rating allows an insurance company to create more accurate rates by shifting higher loss costs to insureds most associated with higher propensities of loss. The rationale behind this is that a credit score is an indicator of financial responsibility. From a fairness perspective the use of a non-driving factor like credit-based insurance score for setting of insurance rates may be perceived to be unfair. Here the fairness concern can also be viewed as an accuracy concern for some subsets of the population. The balance between accuracy and fairness is a frequently discussed subject, which has produced differing regulations across states, as each state takes their own stance. This discussion is not limited to credit-based insurance scores and discussions of disparate impact of data variables will continue to be relevant. |
