sections.title: **1.2.2 Introduction** {#1.2.2-introduction}
sections.content:
In addition to ethical considerations, the work of actuaries is influenced by the regulatory framework in which they work. Laws and regulations exist in part to help protect the rights of individuals, to help assure fair treatment for all people, and to prevent unfair discrimination. There are several laws and regulations that are related to the collection and use of data; it is very important that an actuary is aware of which laws and regulations apply in a given situation. 

Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) are promulgated by the Actuarial Standards Board in the U.S. and help actuaries understand the professional standards applicable to the performance of various actuarial tasks. Other jurisdictions have similar standards. ASOPs covering risk classification, data quality, actuarial communications, and modeling are especially important for the actuary to be aware of in the context of building and implementing predictive models.  
Introduction

sections.title: **1.2.3 Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs)** {#1.2.3-actuarial-standards-of-practice-(asops)}
sections.content:
Actuarial standards of practice (ASOPs) give guidance regarding performing actuarial tasks and describe appropriate communication and disclosure of the results of these tasks. Several ASOPs are directly relevant to the ethical principles and framework previously discussed. Theses ASOPs are required reading.  
Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs)

Component Table15

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 4 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | ASOP 41: Actuarial Communications |
| Tab 1 Content | [ASOP No. 41](#bookmark=id.3ljtm7yemaj) on Actuarial Communications refers to transparency and accountability. ASOP 41 guides communication requirements, including form and content, clarity, timing of communication, and identification of the responsible actuary. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | ASOP 23: Data Quality |
| Tab 2 Content | A key part of accountability is ensuring that the data is of sound quality and fit for purpose before using. [ASOP No. 23](#bookmark=id.fam3nw7b56gv) on Data Quality refers to communication in Section 4 “Communications and Disclosures.” Specifically, it states that any communication regarding data quality should disclose the following: the source(s) of the data, whether the actuary reviewed the data or not (or, if not, any resulting limitations), the extent of the reliance on the data, any material judgments or assumptions, any limitations on the use of the work product based on the data quality, any unresolved concerns that may be material, the existence of results that are highly uncertain or potentially biased due to data quality. As this ASOP notes, transparency around what was and what was not done with the data is critical. The guidance is also closely related to data safety, robustness, and accuracy. |
| Tab 3 Title | Interrelationship Between Transparency and Accountability |
| Tab 3 Text | ASOP 56: Modeling |
| Tab 3 Content | [ASOP No. 56](#bookmark=id.4htq3nk43brb) on Modeling provides guidance on designing, developing, selecting, modifying, using, reviewing, or evaluating models. The ASOP indicates that a model should meet the intended purposes and not be misused or misinterpreted, which relates to model safety. The ASOP also refers to consistency in assumptions, appropriateness of inputs, and mitigation of model risks. It also refers to communication, stating that an actuary should disclose the intended purpose of the model, any material inconsistencies among assumptions in the model, unreasonable output resulting from aggregation of assumptions, other material limitations or known weaknesses, and the extent that the model relied on models developed by other or on experts. ASOP 56 provides some guidance to inform the ethical considerations related to transparency in building predictive models. |
| Tab 4 Title | ASOP 12: Risk Classification |
| Tab 4 Text | ASOP 12: Risk Classification |
| Tab 4 Content | In providing guidance to actuaries in charge of the design of a risk classification system, [ASOP 12](#bookmark=id.i9s2zcuoj0cy) requires that actuaries consider the relationship of the risk characteristics used in the classification system to their outcomes. They should be able to demonstrate that the variation in expected experience correlates to that of the risk characteristic. Selection of risk characteristics should be objectively determined (“it is based on readily verifiable observable facts that cannot be easily manipulated”).  |

sections.title: **1.2.4 Regulations**  {#1.2.4-regulations}
sections.content:
In practice, regulations are strict and must be followed. The law is the law, so aside from interpreting legal language, whether or not an action is compliant isn’t up for debate. 

In the workplace, such compliance involves following the laws and rules that apply to your organization. An organization and its employees must comply with applicable laws and regulations; otherwise there will be consequences such as sanctions, fines, financial losses, or reputational risks. Additionally, organizations often have written policies, processes, and tools that their employees are trained on and expected to follow. These policies, often called a code of conduct, can be stricter than applicable laws and regulations. 

While ethics and regulations both aim for individuals and groups to act morally and responsibly, they are different, yet complementary. In contrast to ethics, laws and regulations are set boundaries that must be complied with and are less open to personal interpretation.  
Regulations

sections.title: **1.2.5 Intersection of Regulations and Ethics**  {#1.2.5-intersection-of-regulations-and-ethics}
sections.content:
Regulations and ethics are ultimately complementary standards that typically work hand in hand. While the most ethical choice is not always clear cut and has trade-offs and conflicts, it is an integral part of compliance with regulations. 

Sometimes it may feel that ethics hold individuals to a higher standard than regulations, but that may not always be the case. While regulations can be viewed as “just the rules” or the minimum that must be followed, there is generally significant time, effort, and thought that went into the creation of those rules. Ethics can be tied to both personal and professional morals and values, which are generally quite broad and overarching. However, there are some situations where laws and regulations can demand more than what is ethically required.  
Intersection of Regulations and Ethics

sections.title: **1.2.6 Regulations on Data Protection and Privacy**  {#1.2.6-regulations-on-data-protection-and-privacy}
sections.content:
Just because you have access to data doesn’t necessarily mean you should or are legally allowed to use it for any purpose. There are regulations and professional standards surrounding the collection and use of data. 

Most regulations are in place to protect consumers. As such, they typically apply only, or at least more forcefully, to “personal data,” i.e., data that can be used to identify an individual. When dealing with personal data (processing, storing, analyzing, or even transferring), there will almost certainly be laws that apply to your activities, and due care should be taken to ensure you are complying with them. 

However, these laws do not usually apply to data that has been anonymized or de-identified to the point at which the data no longer qualifies as personal data and cannot be re-identified. While you might need to anonymize data before you can use it to comply with various laws, the act of anonymization itself is classified as the processing of personal data and needs to comply with the laws governing the use of the data. To comply with these laws, it is important to understand the applicable standards and methods in relation to de-identifying the data.  
Regulations on Data Protection and Privacy

sections.title: **1.2.7 Regulations on Data**  {#1.2.7-regulations-on-data}
sections.content:
Regulations on Data  
In general, any information that can be used to identify an individual (either directly or indirectly), such as a person’s name, social security number, telephone number, or personal address, is considered PII. In some cases, data elements such as birth date or postal code, do not qualify as PII on their own but do constitute PII if used together, as a birth date may be uniquely held in a postal code. What, specifically, is defined as personally identifiable information is subject to legislation. Current laws in your jurisdiction should always be consulted if there are questions.   
Personally identifiable information (PII)   
Laws by Region   
The following pages review data protection laws in some regions. Please note that companies organizations operating in the U.S. will be subject to the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) if the data relates to people in the EU. As such, a responsible approach would be to understand that more than one law from different jurisdictions may apply and seek legal advice as needed.

sections.title: **1.2.8 United States**  {#1.2.8-united-states}
sections.content:
\[BEGIN LINK \-https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa\]  
There is no single principal federal legislation on data protection in the United States. A combination of multiple laws, on both the federal and state level, exist to protect data. While many industries in the United States have seen an immense emergence and growth in the use of big data in recent years, the regulations have not always been able to adapt quickly enough to be relevant for current practices. This difference in practice and regulation can create ethical or legal quandaries. 

Here are some examples of current regulations that exist within the United States. The readings are optional: 

* [CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act)](#bookmark=id.dhr030ij0fkf) relates to personal information  
* [HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)](#bookmark=id.kn42l84uc49v) relates to medical and health information  
* [Privacy Act and Freedom of Information Act](#bookmark=id.13jpjzdmn16m) relates to records held by federal agencies  
* [TCPA (Telephone Consumer Protection Act)](#bookmark=id.dlji3arevln2) relates to telephone calls or texts  
* [GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act)](#bookmark=id.d9hspet5jqc2) applies to the financial industry and private financial information  
* [FCRA (Fair Credit Reporting Act](#bookmark=id.lfso5ityi7ne)) applies to consumer information contained in the files of consumer reporting agencies.

\[END LINK\]  
United States

sections.title: **1.2.9 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act** {#1.2.9-health-insurance-portability-and-accountability-act}
sections.content:
One of the objectives of HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) is to protect the privacy of health and medical information. The U.S. Department of Health & Human Services provides the following paragraph to explain the HIPAA Privacy Rule.  
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act  
The HIPAA Privacy Rule establishes national standards to protect individuals' medical records and other personal health information and applies to health plans, health care clearinghouses, and those health care providers that conduct certain health care transactions electronically. The Rule requires appropriate safeguards to protect the privacy of personal health information and sets limits and conditions on the uses and disclosures that may be made of such information without patient authorization. The Rule also gives patients’ rights over their health information, including rights to examine and obtain a copy of their health records, and to request corrections. (U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, 2020\)

sections.title: **1.2.10 European Union**  {#1.2.10-european-union}
sections.content:
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a data privacy and security law relating to collecting or using data of people in the EU. GDPR is considered the toughest privacy and security law in the world. (Wolford, n.d.). The following provides additional information. 

The General Data Protection Regulation is a European Union law that was implemented May 25, 2018 and requires organizations to safeguard personal data and uphold the privacy rights of anyone in EU territory. The regulation includes seven principles of data protection that must be implemented and eight privacy rights that must be facilitated. It also empowers member state-level data protection authorities to enforce the GDPR with sanctions and fines. (GDPR.eu, 2020\) 

Any organization that processes the personal data of people in the EU must comply with the GDPR. ‘Processing’ is a broad term that covers just about anything you can do with data: collection, storage, transmission, analysis, etc. ‘Personal data’ is any information that relates to a person, such as names, email addresses, I.P. addresses, eye color, political affiliation, and so on. (Proton Technologies AG, n.d.) 

Personal data is any information that relates to an identified or identifiable living individual. Different pieces of information, which collected together can lead to the identification of a particular person, also constitute personal data. Personal data that has been de-identified, encrypted or pseudonymized but can be used to re-identify a person remains personal data and falls within the scope of the GDPR. (European Commission, n.d.)  
European Union

sections.title: **1.2.11 Canada**  {#1.2.11-canada}
sections.content:
Canada has the Privacy Act that sets out privacy rights of personal information and the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) that sets rules on how organizations may collect and use personal information.  
Canada  
Privacy Act   
Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)  
Organizations covered by PIPEDA must generally obtain an individual's consent when they collect, use or disclose that individual's personal information. People have the right to access their personal information held by an organization. They also have the right to challenge its accuracy. 

"Personal information can only be used for the purposes for which it was collected. If an organization is going to use it for another purpose, they must obtain consent again. Personal information must be protected by appropriate safeguards." (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, 2019\)   
"The Privacy Act is the law that sets out \[a person’s\] privacy rights in \[their\] interactions with the federal government. It applies to how the government collects, uses and discloses \[their\] personal information. The Privacy Act protects \[their\] personal information that government institutions hold. The Act also gives \[them\] the right to access \[their\] personal information held by the federal government." (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, 2019\)

sections.title: **1.2.12 Other Countries**  {#1.2.12-other-countries}
sections.content:
Australia and New Zealand   
Australia’s key data protection legislation is the Privacy Act of 1988\. Australia expects to strengthen privacy and data related law. New Zealand has the Privacy Act 2020, which amends the Privacy Act 1993\.  
Other Countries  
Caribbean and Central and South America   
Many Latin American countries apply *habeas dat* *a* as the basic concept underlying data privacy laws. Habeas data is a Latin phrase that translated means “you should have the data.” This is a constitutional right to protect in some Latin American countries. This includes protection of image, privacy, honor, information, self-determination and freedom of information of a person. (Carlos, 2016\) Brazil has enacted a General Data Protection Law (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais or “LGPD”).  
Asia   
Many Asian countries have laws consistent with the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Privacy Framework. The APEC Privacy Framework is a set of non-legally binding principles and guidelines related to privacy protection.  
Africa   
Data protection laws vary across the continent, but many countries have enacted data protection legislation in recent years. There is no unified framework, but many are looking at the EU model as a framework for their country’s legislation.

sections.title: **1.2.13 Laws Defining Protected Classes**  {#1.2.13-laws-defining-protected-classes}
sections.content:
The U.S. has federal anti-discrimination laws defining the following protected classes: 

* Race – Civil Rights Act of 1964  
* Religion – Civil Rights Act of 1964  
* National origin – Civil Rights Act of 1964  
* Age (40 and over) – Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967  
* Sex – Equal Pay Act of 1963 and Civil Rights Act of 1964  
* Sexual orientation and gender identity as of Bostock v. Clayton County – Civil Rights Act of 1964  
* Pregnancy – Pregnancy Discrimination Act  
* Familial status – Civil Rights Act of 1968 Title VIII  
* Disability status – Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990  
* Veteran status – Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act of 1974 and Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act  
* Genetic information – Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act

Laws Defining Protected Classes  
Article 9 of GDPR indicates protected classes as follows: 

* Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited. (European Parliament and Council of European Union, 2016\)

sections.title: **1.2.14 Anti-Discrimination Laws and Regulations**  {#1.2.14-anti-discrimination-laws-and-regulations}
sections.content:
The following list shows some of the laws and regulations to prevent discrimination of individuals in protected classes that apply to different industries in the United States: 

* Credit (e.g., Equal Credit Opportunity Act)  
* Education (e.g., Civil Rights Act of 1964, Education Amendments of 1972\)  
* Employment (e.g., Civil Rights Act of 1964\)  
* Housing (e.g., Fair Housing Act)  
* Insurance (e.g., Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 (“ACA”), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (“HIPAA”), Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (“GINA”), Fair Housing Act, and each state’s regulations in the U.S.)

These laws and regulations may vary based on the domain or context. For example, when one applies for a loan, the U.S. Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, and receipt of public assistance. For personal loans, income level and employment status are important criteria since they can be good signals for future loan payments. However, some of the prohibited attributes are acceptable and used in other domains. For example, age and sex can be used as rating variables for life insurance purposes in most states of the U.S. 

Redlining was an explicit mortgage lending and investment practice that discriminated against people living in predominantly minority communities by using location as a proxy. Redlining, which started in the 1930s as a result of the National Housing Act of 1934, affected mortgages, insurance, other financial services. 

The Fair Housing Act (part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964\) prohibits redlining. While geographic location or zip code is not a directly protected class, there can be a high correlation between zip code and race, ethnicity, national origin, and religion. As such, while credit applications contain the full zip code, loan issuers can use only the first three digits of the zip code in assessing credit-worthiness to prevent redlining.  
Anti-Discrimination Laws and Regulations

sections.title: **1.2.15 Risk Classification in Insurance**  {#1.2.15-risk-classification-in-insurance}
sections.content:
Unlike other industries, insurance is in the business of classifying applicants to the extent the criteria relate to the insurance risk. In some situations, grouping insureds into homogenous classes is considered to be fair when it is based on differences in loss potential and not in a way that discriminates against protected classes. Risk classification attempts to categorize insurance applicants into multiple classes based on risk profiles. The underwriting and risk classification process assigns a risk classification to applicants and declines applications when certain criteria are not met. Without underwriting and risk classification, riskier applicants have an incentive to join the pool, whereas less risky applicants have incentive to not join the pool, leading to adverse selection. Risk classification is a necessary component for the sustainability and soundness of an insurance system. 

Actuarial fairness indicates that the level of premium can differ depending on the level of risk of an individual. Risk classification is a core concept in actuarial practice. Risk classification should be based on data that are reasonable and identify actual drivers of loss. However, it is not true that all predictive variables must be used in risk classification. Many successful products are designed in a manner that rates do not distinguish between certain classes or based on certain characteristics. Problems are more likely to arise if there are unequal or unfair requirements among competitors, which can lead to adverse selection. That is, all competitors should be permitted to use the same variables, where they see fit. Further, the disallowance of protected class variables in risk classification helps to prevent a disproportionate impact on these protected classes that does not reflect an actual greater potential for loss.   
Risk Classification in Insurance

sections.title: **1.2.16 Discrimination in Insurance**  {#1.2.16-discrimination-in-insurance}
sections.content:
While insurance is in the discrimination business, not all discrimination is fair. Certain limits and constraints exist, for example, using factors such as race, national origin,\* and religion. There may be variations in determining factors (e.g., sex) as protected and prohibited for insurance applications. Sex may be relevant to some insurance risks. However, some regions restrict using sex at all for pricing. The EU prohibited the use of sex as a pricing variable effective as of December 21, 2012 (European Commission, 2012). 

In the U.S., insurance companies are regulated at the state level and regulation varies between states. Use of age, sex, and marital status may or may not be allowed in insurance pricing depending on the type of insurance and where the filing is being done. For example, New York State prohibits issuers from discriminating against individuals based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or transgender status. (Department of Financial Services, 2019\) 

\* National origin does not refer to immigration status or citizenship, but rather to heritage.  
Discrimination in Insurance

sections.title: **1.2.17 Considerations for Insurance Laws in the U.S.**  {#1.2.17-considerations-for-insurance-laws-in-the-u.s.}
sections.content:
This page summarizes U.S. insurance law considerations on key attributes (race, national origin, religion, sex\*, sexual orientation, age, credit score, zip code, and genetics) from Understanding Insurance Anti-Discrimination Laws by Avraham, Logue and Schwarcz (Avraham, Logue, & Schwarcz, 2013). The article discussed current state by state laws regarding the use of these key attributes in the five principal lines of insurance—auto, disability, health, life, and property/casualty. 

Click on each tab to read more.  
Considerations for Insurance Laws in the U.S.  
\*In general, this module uses the term “sex” as a biological trait. The article used the term “gender” to indicate sex, as used in this module.

Component Table16

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 5 |
| Tab 1 Title | Race, National Origin, Religion |
| Tab 1 Text | Race, National Origin, Religion |
| Tab 1 Content | As mentioned earlier, race, national origin, and religion are three factors (collectively known as the “Big Three”) with strong restrictions for insurers related to the extent that they can be used in pricing. Ten states have outright prohibitions on the use of these characteristics in all five lines of insurance, with two more forbidding race and national origin but not religion explicitly. Though many states do not contain an outright prohibition on the use of these characteristics uniformly across lines of insurance, the level of regulation regarding these three characteristics in insurance is significantly stricter than any other characteristic. For auto insurance, for example, all states except Montana and Idaho have at least a general restriction on the use of the “Big Three” and the vast majority of states have an outright prohibition.  |
| Tab 2 Title | Sex & Sexual Orientation |
| Tab 2 Text | Sex & Sexual Orientation |
| Tab 2 Content | Restrictions regarding the use of sex in insurance are less strict, overall, than those related to the “Big Three.” In life insurance, it is expressly permitted in all jurisdictions but one (Montana). Some property/casualty insurance products are more restrictive than life insurance. For example, three states have at least a general restriction on the use of sex for personal auto insurance. For disability insurance, only two states expressly permit it, and eleven states have no mention of it. Health insurance has a bimodality in its distribution of laws—18 states expressly permit it, and all but three of the remaining states have a strong limitation or outright prohibition. Most states have no specific regulation on insurance-based discrimination for sexual orientation for any line of insurance. Eighteen states limit or strongly prohibit its use in health insurance, for instance, while all others have no specific law related to it other than a prohibition on generally unfair discrimination. This pattern holds for all other lines of insurance. |
| Tab 3 Title | Age |
| Tab 3 Text | Age |
| Tab 3 Content | Age is much less regulated than the other characteristics discussed so far. Thirty-nine states explicitly permit its use in life insurance, and the remaining states only provide a standard against generally unfair discrimination. Health insurance sees thirty-seven states permit its use, but the laws are less uniform than for life insurance, as several states have specific restrictions. There are several states which have a general restriction on its use in property/casualty insurance, six of which have an outright prohibition. However, for auto insurance, slightly more states trend towards stronger limitations. Disability insurance sees very few limitations across states. It is allowed in five and only has stronger than a general restriction in seven states. No states outright prohibit the use of age for disability insurance.  |
| Tab 4 Title | Credit Score & ZIP Code |
| Tab 4 Text | Credit Score & ZIP Code |
| Tab 4 Content | Credit score and zip code generally have a higher degree of regulation than that of age, but less so than the “Big Three.” There is significant variation across states and across lines of business. For property/casualty, which includes auto insurance, the distribution of laws is bimodal regarding credit score, with clusters around strong limitations and clusters around being expressly permitted. Less bimodality exists for zip code, though with high levels of variation. Health, life, and disability insurance show a large amount of variability in their treatment of both credit score and zip code with no clear pattern between the lines. A substantial number of jurisdictions permit the use of zip code for health insurance, more than the authors of the study expected. The same is true for credit score in health, life, and disability insurance.  |
| Tab 5 Title | Genetics |
| Tab 5 Text | Genetics |
| Tab 5 Content | The use of data from genetic testing is generally more regulated than that of age, but less so than for the “Big Three,” though there is variability across lines of insurance. Sixteen states permit the use of genetic testing for life insurance, and only two states have prohibitions. All but three states prohibit the use of genetic testing in health insurance. Twenty states expressly permit the use of genetic testing in disability insurance. For property/casualty insurance nearly all states have no more than a restriction on generally unfair practices.  |

sections.title: **1.2.18 Guidelines and Principles for Predictive Models**  {#1.2.18-guidelines-and-principles-for-predictive-models}
sections.content:
While there are no explicit regulations for the use of predictive models, there are guidelines and principles available to help direct the usage of big data, artificial intelligence, and predictive models. 

The American Academy of Actuaries (AAA) has recently published a monograph aimed in part at helping actuaries navigate various issues related to big data. (American Academy of Actuaries, 2021\) This paper considers the applications of AI and big data to many aspects of the insurance industry, including distribution, claims, underwriting, reserving, fraud detection, and regulatory oversight. 

The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) has drafted two documents including professional guidelines applicable to the insurance industry, which are summarized here. 

Click on each tab to read more.  
Guidelines and Principles for Predictive Models

Component Table17

| Type | Tabset |
| :---- | :---- |
| Tabs | 2 |
| Tab 1 Title | 3\. A Framework for Ethical Principles |
| Tab 1 Text | Regulatory review of predictive models |
| Tab 1 Content | One source of guidance comes from the Casualty Actuarial and Statistical Task Force, related to the regulatory review of predictive models. This task force has drafted a white paper that proposes changes to the Product Filing Review Handbook to include best practices for the review of predictive models and analytics filed by property and casualty insurers to justify rates (National Association of Insurance Commissioners, 2020b). The paper primarily focuses on personal automobile and home insurance rating plans but concludes the findings should be readily transferrable to other lines of business. It also proposes state guidance (e.g., information, data) for rate filings based on complex predictive models. The white paper also helps to define what is “best practice” and examines current issues in reviewing today’s predictive models. The appendices within the white paper discuss data collection and processing, model building, and the model’s impact on the rating algorithm, including the types of documentation that should be obtained from the insurer to improve transparency. The paper describes current state regulatory activity rather than creating new standards. It is expected that as technology and modeling techniques evolve, individual states will need to determine how to review the new approaches (National Association of Insurance Commissioners, 2020b). The white paper was adopted by the NAIC on April 14, 2021\. |
| Tab 2 Title | 4\. Actuarial Standards of Practice (ASOPs) |
| Tab 2 Text | Principles on artificial intelligence |
| Tab 2 Content | Another source of guidance from the NAIC is a document outlining principles on artificial intelligence (“A.I.”). This guidance comes from the Innovation and Technology Task Force, and serves to “inform and establish general expectations for A.I. actors and systems, emphasizing the importance of accountability, compliance, transparency, and safe, secure and robust outputs” (National Association of Insurance Commissioners, 2020a). This document provides assistance to regulators and NAIC committees regarding insurance specific applications, surrounding big data, modeling, artificial intelligence, and similar analysis. The document uses “FACTS” as a means of accommodating and protecting innovation, while protecting consumers from risks and harm. This FACTS approach is:  Fair and ethical Accountable Compliant Transparent Secure, safe and robust  |

sections.title: **1.2.19 Module Summary**  {#1.2.19-module-summary}
sections.content:
While ethics and regulations are individual concepts, they ultimately are interrelated and closely associated with one another. This module discussed that in working in analytics, it is important to ensure work is done ethically, as well as compliance with any applicable regulations.  
Module Summary

sections.title: **1.2.20 Ethical Principles and Framework** {#1.2.20-ethical-principles-and-framework}
sections.content:
This module reviewed three groups of principles: fairness, safety, and transparency and accountability. These are used to guide discussions in later sections, where they are applied to the overall process, data, analytics, models, and implementation and governance.  
Ethical Principles and Framework  
Insurance Regulations   
Unlike many other industries, insurance is in the business of risk categorization to the extent it relates to the insurance risk. This is when discrimination is considered fair and risk classification occurs. However, certain limits and constraints exist, for example, using classification factors such as race, national origin, and religion. There may be variations in determining factors (e.g., sex) as protected and prohibited for insurance applications, depending on domicile or type of products.  
Comparison Between Ethical and Legal Issues   
Ethics refers to standards of behavior defining how individuals, a community, or society should act morally and responsibly in various situations they may find themselves in. Regulations are strict and must be followed. Regulations set a boundary for what one can or cannot do. There may be cases where certain actions are both ethical and legal. However, legality does not guarantee ethicality or vice versa.  
Key Relevant Regulations Related to Data Protection, Privacy, And Anti-Discrimination   
This module noted that regulations exist to regulate privacy, data collection and use, and discrimination. Discrimination against certain groups, attributes, or categories is illegal and regulated in many countries.  
ASOPs   
This module reviewed four Actuarial Standards of Practice that apply directly to the aforementioned ethical principles and framework. ASOPs 41 (Actuarial Communications), 23 (Data Quality), 56 (Modeling), and 12(Risk Classification) provide guidance that can be applied in the context of actuarial model building.

sections.title: **1.3.2 Introduction** {#1.3.2-introduction}
sections.content:
In this section the concepts covered in the previous two sections will be reinforced through a case study. Thoughtfully consider the questions asked prior to viewing the suggested answers.  
Introduction

sections.title: **1.3.3 Business Context** {#1.3.3-business-context}
sections.content:
You are an actuary working in the underwriting department of EZ Life, a life insurance company operating in the United States that specializes in selling term life insurance products. In recent years, management has expressed a desire to streamline the risk classification process that supports the pricing of its individual term life business. 

EZ Life’s goal is to do this by using available policy characteristics that will be collected during underwriting such as information on the application and information that can easily be collected via electronic means such as pharmacy and motor vehicle records. You plan to assess feasibility by using information that has already been collected by underwriting and resides in their administration system for current and former policyholders, or characteristics that could be easily obtained, to predict the results of key medical tests. You and several recent hires with background in predictive modeling provide the perfect opportunity to do that based on the skill set you have brought to EZ Life. Management has asked your team to create a new predictive underwriting model to accomplish their goal.   
Business Context

sections.title: **1.3.4 Problem Definition** {#1.3.4-problem-definition}
sections.content:
The development of the new predictive underwriting model has taken on a certain urgency by EZ Life’s Board, and they want the results as quickly as possible. EZ Life has the capacity to conduct new medical exams; the results of a few key tests from these will be used in the predictive model as the target variable that the model will be trying to predict. If your model can predicting those test results accurately, then there will be no need to conduct those tests, leading to significant cost reductions. A remaining issue is which variables should be used as predictors of the results of the medical exams. EZ Life also is trying to decide between several different predictive algorithms to use in the creation of its final model.  
Business Context

sections.content:
The underwriting team held a brainstorming session on possible data that may be available or could be collected to help them in the development of this new model. The variables identified in the brainstorming session are shown on the right. 

Which of these data fields would be acceptable to use in the analysis from a regulatory perspective, and which fields may have regulatory issues if used?   
Question

| Title | Panel |
| Header | Variables |
| Content |  Facial photo Hobby Smoking status (vaping included) Genetic testing results Property tax paying record Credit score Disability status Age (and birthdate) Race Body Mass Index (BMI)  Family medical history Job Residence street address and zip code Homeownership Income level Education level Policy size Name Sex Sexual orientation  |
| Footer | Panel Footer |

Component Table28

| Type | Panel |
| :---- | :---- |
| Title | Panel |
| Header | Sample Answer  |
| Content |  Some of these data fields have standard uses in individual life insurance pricing and underwriting and would not cause any issues with regulators or the public at large due to their history. Among these are sex (in most states), age, and smoking status. Other fields explicitly deal with the health of the potential insured and would not lead to any ethical complaints due to traditional underwriting practices already in place. These fields include body mass index and disability status. Family history of cancer or other medical conditions is also something widely collected and does not see many existing regulatory issues in the U.S. market at this time. Other fields have explicit prohibitions on their use in life insurance pricing in certain jurisdictions. Among these are sexual orientation, race or even sex in the case of the state of Montana in the United States. There are certain fields that may have some predictive value in setting rates for life insurance, but which are deemed unacceptable as a basis for pricing by the societal context in which an organization operates. These will vary by both time and place but could include variables such as homeownership or income level. |
| Footer | Panel Footer |

sections.title: **1.3.6 Question**  {#1.3.6-question}
sections.content:
The underwriting team went ahead and collected data based on their discussions and added it to the administration system. The IT team then provided the data from that system to the predictive modeling team. The data science team developed a predictive model using a model that the underwriting team members were not familiar with. The model used the average of a set of thousands of decision trees. The predictive results were considered significantly more accurate than the simpler models that were used in the past. Using mean squared error as the accuracy measurement, it was found that the new model was 15% more accurate. 

Describe possible concerns with the model from transparency and interpretability aspects.  
Question

Component Table29

| Type | Panel |
| :---- | :---- |
| Title | Panel |
| Header | Sample Answer  |
| Content |  A model that isn’t familiar to the team using it opens itself up to many interpretability and transparency issues. Accuracy is certainly a priority when building a predictive model, but if the model is more accurate but less interpretable to management, then its uptake will be much more difficult. If unusual results emerge from the model during its use, the underwriting team will not be able to explain the drivers of those results and the confidence that the model was, in fact, more accurate, rather than overfitted to sample data, will be lost. Another issue of transparency relates to the increased complexity that is introduced into a model by unintentional interactions between variables. If any of the variables are included in error or don’t have actual predictive power in the final model but create an unintentional correlation with other variables, this may muddy even further the interpretability of the model and its components. Some of the variables included may also be correlated with illegal or undesirable model variables which could be problematic. |
| Footer | Panel Footer |

sections.title: **1.3.7 Question** {#1.3.7-question}
sections.content:
The underwriting team moved forward and deployed the predictive model. To monitor the accuracy of the results, the team is considering performing medical exams on a subset of applicants. 

The team is considering a few options to select the subset. They could offer a premium discount to those who volunteer for the medical exams. Alternatively, they could reach out to and request participation in the medical exams from randomly selected applicants. Finally, they could offer their request for medical exams only to those with a face amount higher than $1 million. 

Describe why any of the options are ethically appropriate and describe why some are inappropriate.   
Question

Component Table30

| Type | Panel |
| :---- | :---- |
| Title | Panel |
| Header | Sample Answer  |
| Content |  **Premium Discount**: Premium discounts for fully underwritten vs. simple underwriting have a long history in the industry and will likely not raise ethical concerns for the bonus itself. One ethical issue that could arise through offering bonuses to volunteers for a study is that there is a high likelihood that demand will exceed supply. Not every policyholder will be able to participate, in which case either the bonus is still paid out without an exam being performed or, more likely and the ethical issue at hand, the promised bonuses will have to be denied. This could be handled with an express limit on participation spelled out in the offer but otherwise creates issues. The ethical framework also lists accuracy as a core ethical value, and a volunteer-based collection effort will seriously impact the accuracy of results due to the potential for skewed results. **Request participation**: This is likely to be ethically appropriate. The list of potential participants is randomly selected which helps satisfy the ethical demands of accuracy. **Exams offered to those with high face**: Higher face amounts have traditionally been afforded a higher degree of underwriting, so there isn’t likely an ethical issue on that front. This, however, does create another issue with accuracy of results since existing high face amount business likely already underwent more underwriting and the subsequent exams will not be representative. |
| Footer | Panel Footer |
